title: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says
description: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.Ukra
body: Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with President Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles.Ukraine said strikes on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia - which killed seven people and injured at least 24 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally.In Voronezh, western Russia, warehouses of the biggest online retailer Wildberries were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks.The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border.In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea"."The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world.He has not presented any evidence to back up his comments. It is not the first time Zelensky as well as other senior Ukrainian and Western officials have accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea.Ukraine's military has said that says dozens of North Korean missiles have been fired by Russia into its territory since Moscow's full-scale invasion in February 2022.The Ukrainian president warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Some 11,000 North Korean soldiers were deployed to help Moscow push Ukrainian troops out of the western Russian region of Kursk following their cross-border incursion in August 2024.In January 2025, Western officials told the BBC that North Korean troops had suffered nearly 40% casualties in the fighting there in just three months.In his Monday's address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military.He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary".Zaporizhzhia regional head Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs.All seven casualties were employees of Ukraine's Zaporizhstal metallurgical plant, which later halted all its operations.One person was injured in strikes on the capital Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires.Local officials later said a children's hospital was damaged - but there were no injuries as staff and patients were sheltering. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on the north-eastern Ukrainian city of Sumy, according to regional head Serhii Kryvosheienko.He later said that one person was killed when Russia attacked the city with gliding bombs in the afternoon.Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages.Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted.It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors.Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Wildberries in the Voronezh region.Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated.In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses.Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army.The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery.Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.The Uzbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan.

schema.headline: Russia using North Korean missiles to strike Ukraine, Zelensky says

title: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA
description: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the top
body: Last month, Cunningham, one of the league's most high-profile players, gave an interview to ESPN, external in which the conversation turned to the topic of "protecting" women's sports.The Indiana Fever guard said she had received criticism from people who believed she "hated" transgender people, something she denied.She said she wanted to "extend love" to everyone, but added: "I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."She later doubled down on her comments, saying it was "common sense", external to bar transgender athletes from competing in women's sports.Her words quickly moved beyond basketball and into a wider political debate in the United States.President Donald Trump expressed his support for Cunningham, while vice-president JD Vance said she was "inspiring".Though the 29-year-old later said she is "not a very political person", her remarks have followed her around the country. Competing rallies from critics and supporters were organised at Indiana's games, along with small-scale protests.The scale of the debate in the media, online and in politics was striking given no openly transgender woman is due to play, or has ever played, in the WNBA.The WNBA operates under a collective bargaining agreement (CBA), a deal negotiated between the league and its players association (WNBPA), setting rules on matters including player salary caps, revenue sharing, benefits and overall league operations.On player eligibility, the CBA states: "Only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA."The WNBA has yet to comment publicly on the row since Cunningham's comments but league commissioner Cathy Engelbert reportedly sent a memo to teams last week in which she said the matter would be discussed at an upcoming pre-arranged meeting with team presidents.In the memo, seen by the Associated Press, external, Engelbert said the league would "always approach this topic thoughtfully, respectfully, and in alignment with the longstanding values of our league".She added: "Our player eligibility rules, unlike the eligibility rules of some other leagues and governing bodies, are collectively bargained. Preserving the integrity of our game and ensuring fair competition will always remain among the league's highest priorities."However, the lack of detail in the league's eligibility criteria has been brought to light by Kanter Freedom, who finished his playing career with the Boston Celtics in 2022."If simply declaring who you are is all that's required, then I meet every single requirement necessary to compete in the WNBA," he wrote on Instagram, external.Kanter Freedom, who has previously spoken out about human rights violations in China and Turkey, among other issues, added: "I know my presence on the court will stir up strong opinions. I am definitely not here to mock, make fun of, or disrespect any community or personal choices."I'm simply asking that the current rules be applied equally to everyone - the rules that represent the very values many WNBA players and coaches have publicly advocated for."A day after Kanter Freedom's 'announcement', Royce White - who made three appearances in the NBA as a player and is now a Republican Senate candidate - said he would also declare for the Draft, adding: "I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball."Whether the vagueness of the rules are by design to leave it open to transgender women or a sign of an oversight that genuinely needs tightening up is not clear.BBC Sport has contacted Cunningham's representatives, the WNBA and WNBPA for comment.Cunningham's comments have become a flashpoint inside a league which has a long history of player activism on issues including race, gender equality and LGBTQ+ rights.The players' association did not mention Cunningham by name when it eventually addressed the debate.In a statement the WNBPA denounced "hate abuse and demonisation of the transgender community" and reaffirmed its commitment to "justice, equity, diversity and inclusion".It called on fans to report abusive behaviour at games and added that it would continue to have "hard" conversations but it "will not be used as political pawns".There is strong feeling on both sides of the argument. Minnesota Lynx head coach and president Cheryl Reeve, who said: "I come from a space of inclusion."The narrative that I think is problematic is to suggest that transgender athletes are the biggest problem in women's sports."Reeve wore a "Trans Kids Belong" T-shirt before Minnesota played Indiana earlier this month and was seen speaking to Cunningham on court before the game.Cunningham later said the pair had exchanged their perspectives and that the conversation ended with "love and respect".Golden State Valkyries forward Gabby Williams said she would welcome a transgender athlete "on my team or against my team, any time".Last month, the WNBA suspended Seattle Storm co-owner Celeste Keaton from attending the team's next five home games after an exchange with two fans, who were sat courtside displaying signs thanking Cunningham for "speaking up for girls".Keaton reportedly confronted the teenage fans and admonished them during the game. The Storm have since apologised.As for Cunningham, the attention has increasingly become an unwelcome distraction.Having defended her original comments, she said recently that she now wanted the conversation to return to what was happening on court."I want to get back to basketball, it's always been about basketball" she said, arguing that the standard of play in the WNBA was being overshadowed by issues away from the game.But that may prove difficult, as pressure grows on the league to clarify exactly who is eligible to play.In recent years, many governing bodies in sport have amended their rules about the inclusion of transgender athletes at the elite level, moving more towards restrictions.Athletics, cycling and aquatics, for example, have implemented outright bans on transgender women taking part in women's events.In March, it was announced that the women's category of Olympic sports will be limited to biological females from the LA Olympic Games in 2028.The International Olympic Committee (IOC) says eligibility will be determined by a "once-in-a-lifetime" sex test, which would prevent transgender women and those with differences in sexual development (DSD) who have gone through male puberty from competing.In the United States, transgender women and girls are banned from competing in women's sports categories in schools, universities and the grassroots level.That was part of an executive order - titled "Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports" - signed by President Trump last year. It does not cover professional sport.

schema.headline: The transgender controversy surrounding the WNBA

title: Trump's secret plane swap highlights personal stakes of Iran war
description: "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonatha
body: "I got him before he got me. They tried twice. Well, I got him first."That was President Donald Trump's observation, made to ABC correspondent Jonathan Karl, in a phone conversation the day after he launched the US military campaign against Iran in FebruaryAn Israeli airstrike, conducted with US approval and co-ordination, had just killed the Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian leaders – and Trump drew a direct line from that attack to threats and alleged plots the Iranians had made against him in previous years.Trump has refrained from similar remarks in the ensuing six months of warfare, but Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has echoed the view."Iran tried to kill President Trump, and President Trump got the last laugh," he said in March, noting that an unnamed Iranian who he said led an assassination unit had been killed in US strikes.These comments hint at the personal nature of this war – and the concerns by the president and his security team of the threat Iran still poses to his safety.Those concerns were dramatically illustrated by this week's revelation that Trump secretly switched to an alternate aircraft on his flight back from the Nato summit in Turkey last month. He left the media and most of the White House staff to depart on the presidential Air Force One 747 jet, which became, essentially, a decoy.It was an elaborate ruse, which included the president being transported to and from aircraft inside a catering truck, in response to what American officials reportedly believed to be credible intelligence of an Iranian missile threat to Air Force One.The White House has given little detail about this threat - but nonetheless it marks another striking episode in the turbulent history of Trump's relationship with Iran.Government security experts have said such measures are not unusual when a president travels in or near a warzone. Past presidents have travelled to places like Afghanistan, Iraq and Ukraine under cover of secrecy – but never without at least some prior knowledge by media outlets, under agreements that they would not disclose the movement until after the fact.The optics of Trump hiding in a catering truck from an apparent Iranian threat are less than ideal for a president who has repeatedly touted his strength - as well as the frailty of Iran's military after months of war.The secrecy in the days and weeks after the Secret Service operation in Ankara may have been, in part, to avoid undermining his public image of power.The operation, which took more than a month to come to light, also underscores the apparent threat Iran continues to present to US interests in a conflict that the president asserts is all but wrapped up against an adversary he has said has been thoroughly defeated on the battlefield.Iranian threats against Trump are not new, however.After Trump, in his first term, ordered the January 2020 missile strike that killed Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) leader Qasem Soleimani, Iran's leaders promised reprisals against the American president and senior administration leaders.In one instance, an Iranian mural depicted a drone targeting Trump while he played golf in Florida.It appears that there were more to these Iranian threats than just posturing.The Biden administration warned Iran in 2022 not to target any US citizens, after unearthing a plan to target former Trump National Security Adviser John Bolton.And in July 2024, US law enforcement arrested a Pakistani man, Asif Merchant, who allegedly had ties to the IRGC, for plotting to kill Trump. Four months later, an Afghani citizen, Farhad Shakeri, was charged with another assassination scheme against Trump.Merchant was convicted in March 2026, but Shakeri, who US prosecutors allege was directed by an IRGC official, is still at large.Although these attempts were foiled during the planning stages, the physical risks Trump faced as he sought a return to the White House were all too apparent. In July 2024 he was left bloodied after a gunman opened fire at a rally in Butler, Pennsylvania. Two months later, an armed man was arrested in Florida after US Secret Service agents spotted him hiding in the trees near where Trump was playing golf."It was a galvanising moment for him," Maggie Haberman, a White House correspondent for the New York Times, said in a recent interview, external when discussing both the Iranian plots and assassination attempts of 2024. "All of that in his mind becomes one big blur.""For Trump himself, Iran and this feeling of being under threat is constant," she said.The president, according to the news website Semafor, external, often muses - and jokes - about becoming a target of assassination."Nobody told me how dangerous it is to be president, and if they had told me, I probably wouldn't have run," one White House official recounted Trump as saying. "And he makes comments like that in jest, but there's a reality behind that."Trump's bombing of Iran's nuclear research facilities in 2025, and this year's expansive bombing campaign and naval blockade, prompted a new round of Iranian threats against Trump – and a direct warning by the US president in response.In July, Trump wrote on Truth Social that Iran had made threats "to assassinate, or attempt to assassinate" him and said 1,000 "missiles are Locked and Loaded and aimed at the Islamic Republic of Iran, with thousands more to immediately follow, should the Iranian Government act on its threat".The president's message to Iran was blunt. Many of the recent threats against him have been unequivocal, too.At the funeral service for Khamenei, held the day before Trump departed Turkey, participants carried a banner that read "#KillTrump". The following week, in a square in central Tehran, a building featured a large mural of the American president, lying in a black coffin, with the words "We will kill Trump" and "Blood for blood" written below it.Iran has denied involvement in any previous plots against Trump, but the message – delivered after Khamenei's death and reports of Iranian civilian casualties in US and Israeli strikes – has been clear.The war, Iranians are saying, is far from over. And Trump, himself, is a target for revenge.On the final leg of the journey back to the US from Turkey, as Trump and his travelling media pool were reunited on the same aircraft, the president came back to the press cabin to talk to reporters.They asked about the unusual journey, which included an order by the Secret Service that the window shades on the decoy plane be closed during takeoff from Ankara."I have read all the time I'm number one on their list," he told them. "But if I go, you go, right?"

schema.headline: Trump's secret plane swap highlights personal stakes of Iran war

title: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift
description: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaic
body: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is under fire for comments he made about two melons gifted to him by his Japanese counterpart Sanae Takaichi, after a former Japanese envoy called it an insult.During an appearance on the Bush Deep podcast, Albanese gestured near his chest while referring to the crown melons, calling them "pretty strange" gifts that "ended up being quite good".That episode, which aired in July, had already landed the PM in hot water because of "inappropriate" comments he made about popstar Kylie Minogue.Opposition leaders are now demanding he apologise to Takaichi, but Albanese's position is that it was the host who made the joke, not him, the BBC understands.While discussing the melons Takaichi's team had presented to Albanese during her visit to Australia in May, the host of Bush Deep, comedian Nikki Osborne, quipped: "She brought two... She just came in looking like Pamela Anderson.""She brought two, and they are beautiful," Albanese responded.The exchange, which drew relatively little interest when the episode aired, has resurfaced after Tokyo's former ambassador to Canberra Shingo Yamagami labelled Albanese's comments a "sexist joke" and said they "betrayed the close bond" between Japan and Australia."The last thing [Takaichi] expected was to be so casually mocked by the trusted leader of Japan's special strategic partner," he wrote in an opinion piece published by The Australian on Monday.Crown melons are the "most prized fruit" in Japan and "treasured as something special", Yamagami added, noting that a single melon costs more than 30,000 yen ($188)."So, prime minister, please enjoy Japan's sweet and juicy melons without thinking about a woman's anatomy, and instead focus on what our two countries must do together," he said.During his two-year stint in Australia, Yamagami had a notably frosty relationship with some members of Albanese's Labor Party over disagreements regarding China.An opposition MP asked Albanese on Tuesday if he would apologise for the "foul-mouthed, classless comments about women", to which the prime minister said he "rejected the assertion of the question".He went on: "Australia and Japan have never been closer. My government has taken our special strategic partnership to new heights."Australia's opposition leader Angus Taylor on Monday also criticised the gaffe as "insulting", and demanded that Albanese make a personal apology.Several Labor ministers have jumped to Albanese's defence, saying the former envoy and the media have misinterpreted his comments.Finance Minister Katy Gallagher said the remarks "were not intended to be interpreted the way that our political opponents and some media outlets are reporting".Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek called it "a completely unnecessary interpretation of what the prime minister said". "I think people watching it for themselves can make their own minds up," Plibersek told Australia's Channel Seven.Plibersek had earlier defended Albanese's controversial remarks about Minogue as nothing more than a sign that he was a fan.The prime minister drew a wave of condemnation early last month after Osborne asked him on the podcast whether he would "shag, marry or date" Kylie Minogue, actress Nicole Kidman or entertainer Rhonda Burchmore, to which he replied "Kylie, clearly... all of the above".Albanese later issued a public apology, saying: "I apologise unequivocally for the comments".Osborne, who is best known for posting crude comedy sketches on YouTube, launched her podcast series earlier this year. Her podcast site describes her as a "wildly inappropriate journalist" who asks "questions no one else would dare".

schema.headline: Australia PM Anthony Albanese under fire for remarks over Sanae Takaichi's melon gift

title: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health
description: President Donald Trump said a former US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released."A
body: President Donald Trump said a former US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released."After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place.Robert Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested in 2022 for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state.Gilman was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration.The BBC understands Gilman is expected to arrive early on Wednesday morning at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated.Trump said he spoke to Gilman on the phone, "and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" "During my Administration, we have prioritised bringing home Americans detained abroad, and have done so at a level never seen before," Trump added.Kieran Ramsey, chief investigative officer for Global Reach, the advocacy group representing the former Marine, told Reuters that Gilman was released because the Russian government realised "they're not losing any geopolitical power position by releasing him. This is a humanitarian release".Gilman served in the US Marines for a year until August 2020.He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years.He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was increased to 10 years.In Russian confinement, Gilman was subjected to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson of  Global Reach told CBS, the BBC's US media partner.The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson.He said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian and Chuck Zimmerman."While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X."The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he continued.

schema.headline: Russia releases former US Marine reported in poor health

title: Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia
description: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against hu
body: A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war.It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to the Russian capital, Moscow, with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power.Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence.Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule.In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces.That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed.Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year.Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial.He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death".The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell.The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij.Outside the courthouse after the ruling, hundreds of people of all ages gathered holding pictures of their loved ones who were killed by the regime.Crowds were clapping and chanting, while cars drove by excitedly honking their horns.A group of men passed out flags."The joy is indescribable," one man told the BBC, hoisting up a photo of his late father. "God willing we will see Bashar al-Assad and all his aides hanging on the gallows."Another woman told the BBC everyone is feeling a mix of "victory and liberation.""The voices of the victims are finally heard. Justice has been achieved!" she exclaimed.Nouha al-Masri, a prosecutor in the case, lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at al-Omari Square in Deraa."We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us," Masri told the BBC."Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward."It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow.It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership.An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture.He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty.Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia.Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions.Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994.Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war.Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus and Leen Alsaadi, BBC Arabic in Deraa.

schema.headline: Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad sentenced to death in absentia

title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
description: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MM
body: US President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots."Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.Medical experts have criticised the new order and said it could reduce vaccination rates and expose children to harmful diseases.The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).Trump's order serves as guidance, not a mandate, since shots required for school attendance are set at the state level, rather than by the federal government.The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox."We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."The president suggested the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body. According to the FDA, external, a single dose of MMR is 0.5ml.When a reporter asked for evidence of the "lethal" claim, Trump said: "What I've heard is that there are some people that say it is that way."According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), external, the MMR vaccine carries a very small risk of febrile seizures for young children. Those with health issues, including severe allegeric reactions or weakened immune systems, are advised to consult with healthcare providers before taking the shots.The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".According to the CDC, there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots". Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.Dr William Schaffner of the Vanderbilt University School of Medicine in Nashville told the BBC the increased number of visits would be harder for parents and providers to track and would add to the expense without any scientific benefit.Since taking office in 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr has sought to change and loosen vaccine regulations. During a tense 20-minute interview on CNN last week, Kennedy insisted he had "never questioned the efficacy of the MMR vaccine".He said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.Trump administration officials have said the order means children in the US would receive much less than the 72 shots recommended under the previous vaccine schedule, a figure that assumes annual flu and Covid-19 doses.Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, said Trump's executive order was "dangerous" and not based on "gold-standard science"."Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said. Republican Senator Bill Cassidy, who was the deciding vote in the Senate to confirm Kennedy as health secretary, also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong"."The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, a physician, wrote on X. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism."Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles.Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism.On its website, the CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six.How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP.There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says.Trump's order also calls for the development of alternatives to aluminium in vaccines, and to test if those alternatives are safer and more effective.But the AAP, external says studies have found no significant health risks associated with the tiny amounts of aluminium salts in vaccines.Small amounts of aluminium salts - which are found naturally in soil, water and foods - have been used in some vaccines for decades in order to boost the body's immune response. That means lesser quantities of the vaccine and fewer doses are needed, according to AAP.

schema.headline: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots

title: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake
description: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquak
body: Rescue workers in Colombia are working against the clock to free survivors trapped in buildings and under rubble following Monday's powerful earthquake. More than 180 people have been confirmed dead - most in the cities of Cali and Pereira. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) on Monday and was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia - with fresh aftershocks still being felt on Tuesday.  While the official death toll remains 181, an aggregated figure gathered from local officials puts it higher - potentially at more than 240. A state of emergency has been declared by President Abelardo de la Espriella. Giving an update on Tuesday from Pereira, one of the worst hit cities, President Espriella said as well as those killed, almost 2,600 had been injured, and almost 200 people remain missing. He also reported that more than 1,100 homes had been destroyed, and more than 8,000 had been damaged. Overnight on Monday into Tuesday, several people several people spent the night outdoors in cities like Pereira and Cali - either due to their homes being destroyed, or fear of further collapses. Across the country, dozens of larger buildings have also collapsed. In Cali, a city of 2.2 million people where there have been 95 deaths, a unified command post has been set up to co-ordinate the rescue effort. On Tuesday, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said that 239 people remained trapped, with 949 injured and 45 buildings which have either completely or partially collapsed. Several of the upper floors of one of the city's hospitals, some dedicated to paediatric care, collapsed, leaving some patients trapped.In Calima, a neighbourhood in the north of Cali, four children died after a section of the Gimnasio Calima school collapsed.  The mayor of the municipality, Antonio Cadavid, stated that other children ended up with serious injuries, with a total of 30 children were referred to care centres.To combat threats of looting, he has also ordered a curfew, coming into effect at 20:00 local time, and lasting until 06:00 on Wednesday morning. Hours after the earthquake hit Pereira, a resident of the Parque Industrial neighborhood, near the city's airport, told BBC Mundo about the shock being experienced in the area."It's impossible to get around the city center. In Bolívar Square (the city's main square), at least one building collapsed. Furthermore, there are structures where buses and trucks are trapped, and people are afraid those structures will collapse as well," he said."We're all in shock. It was really awful."Jorge Eduardo Rojas, mayor of Manizales, said five people had been killed in the city. Sixty buildings in Manizales had partially or totally collapsed. Cautioning about further aftershocks, Rojas urged the public not to share chain messages or social media posts from unknown sources, as they "may contain false or unverified information... which could cause greater concern and alarm among the public".  On Tuesday, help and support continued to be offered to Colombia from the international community. A statement from a spokesperson for UN Secretary-General, António Guterres, stated that he "expresses his solidarity with the people and government of Colombia" and that it working to support the government's response.   Spain's Foreign Minister, José Manuel Albares, reported that 164 Spaniards were still missing.At the moment, he added, there are no reports of injuries or deaths of its citizens.The Donald Trump administration, which backed President Abelardo de la Espriella in his successful election earlier this year, announced this afternoon a donation of $15.5m (£11.5m) to Colombia.Offers of help have also come from Ecuador, Brazil, El Salvador, and Venezuela.

schema.headline: Rescuers scramble for survivors with 180 dead in Colombia earthquake

title: Assam: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana raft
description: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar ByInd
body: Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar ByIndia correspondentWell past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother.Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety."Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says.An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts.The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves.By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it.Image caption, Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandryThe scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam.The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps.The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated.For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound."This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says.Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime.Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km.Image caption, A 97-year-old Lokada Duarah was carried onto a banana tree trunk and taken to safety after floodwaters rose around her homeImage source, Anadolu via Getty ImagesImage caption, A boy uses a makeshift banana raft to navigate floodwaters in AssamShe had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building.Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'.Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it.She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed.None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says.The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly.Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages.About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp.Image caption, Baruah and her family abandoned their home nearly a day after the water began risingFor five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil.Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats.  Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill.But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before?Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley,  a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms".The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, A family shelters inside a tent in Sivasagar district, among more than 5,000 people lodged in 252 relief campsImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Amit Giri holds a photo of his father, Siv Sankar Giri, who died in the floods, outside their damaged home in Sivasagar. He is among 100 people killed in the floods.As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251.In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat.Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology.Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam."What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography.For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal.Image caption, Only 60 of Baruah's goats survived the floodsShe has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week.Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have.So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life.She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance.Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee?"No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before.""We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

schema.headline: Assam: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana raft

title: Luigi Mangione murder trial to have anonymous jury
description: The jury in the New York state trial of Luigi Mangione will remain anonymous, the judge overseeing the case ruled on Tuesday.Mangione has pleaded not
body: The jury in the New York state trial of Luigi Mangione will remain anonymous, the judge overseeing the case ruled on Tuesday.Mangione has pleaded not guilty to the killing of UnitedHealthcare chief executive Brian Thompson outside a Manhattan hotel in December 2024. The case has been at the centre of an online frenzy between Mangione's backers - many of whom see the 28-year-old as a symbol of the backlash against US healthcare costs - and his critics, who analyse his intentions and possible political views. In Tuesday's hearing, Judge Gregory Carro decided the 12-person jury would be anonymous to the public because of the intense spotlight on the case.Mangione attended the final pre-trial hearing dressed in a charcoal grey suit with his hair clipped short. He sat silently at the defence table while his attorneys conferred with the judge. The trial begins next month, with jury selection scheduled to start on 8 September.Mangione, if found guilty, could face decades behind bars. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges, including second-degree murder and weapons-related offences. He faces a separate federal trial next year, in which he has also pleaded not guilty.Here's what to know about the upcoming trial, and what questions remain.

schema.headline: Luigi Mangione murder trial to have anonymous jury

title: How South East Asia's 'ghost city' became a Trojan horse for scammers
description: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved inFigure caption, Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost townBy
body: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved inFigure caption, Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost townByGavin ButlerReporting fromForest City, MalaysiaFrom a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust."In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties."If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people ‌and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations.The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response.Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising.Image source, BBC/ Gavin ButlerImage caption, Forest City was meant to house some 700,000 residents - but the current population is thought to be less than 1% of that"The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure."Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams. Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse.Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified.But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense. Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours.Image source, BBC/ Gavin ButlerImage caption, Forest City's sales gallery features a gigantic diorama of the complex in miniatureKevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions."We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special."Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city"."When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000"."That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests."They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here."Image source, BBC/ Gavin ButlerImage caption, Shuttered buildings and dilapidated infrastructure are a common sight in Forest CityThere are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City.Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients. Featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park, the resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand.But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill.The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home.And that appears to  have made the complex a honeypot for scammers."Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says."Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed."With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs.Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking.Image source, BBC/ Gavin ButlerImage caption, The complex sits on Malaysia's southernmost tip, less than five kilometres (three miles) from SingaporeFor all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures. Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively.Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate".Such power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways.Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions.Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work."It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread".The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia.Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur.Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention".Image source, BBC/ Gavin ButlerImage caption, The $100-billion dollar complex's quiet streets and deserted beaches have earned it a reputation as a "ghost city"In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging.Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective".He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars."For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary."Other residents feel the same way.Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection."Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen."He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City.One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be."So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five."

schema.headline: How South East Asia's 'ghost city' became a Trojan horse for scammers

title: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight
description: On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.But when the
body: On 8 July, US President Donald Trump boarded Air Force One in plain sight of television cameras as he departed the Nato summit in Turkey.But when the mighty Boeing aircraft left Ankara, the president had reportedly already been secretly spirited away via a catering truck to a C-32A, a military version of the Boeing 757, which flew the president to RAF Mildenhall in the UK.Those left on board were unwitting decoys and had no indication that Trump was no longer travelling with them. But deception of this kind is not unusual."That's very common," said Ronald Kessler, an author who has written extensively on the agency. "There's a long history of strategies to mislead anybody who might be trying to harm the president."Robert McDonald, a former high-ranking Secret Service agent with experience working on presidential security details, told the BBC that smaller-scale deceptions are used frequently during motorcade operations.These motorcades - which often include dozens of security and support vehicles, as well as ambulances and vans carrying White House reporters - typically include two "Beasts", as the enhanced limousine carrying the president is known.While one vehicle carries the president, the other travels nearby as a decoy, switching locations while en route to the destination."It's what we call a shell game," said McDonald, who drove one of the vehicles during President George W Bush's administration. "Even in DC if we headed to Andrews [Joint Base Andrews - where Air Force One flies from], those two limousines would change position, like under a highway overpass." "But that would happen out of sight of anybody other than those in the motorcade or in that tunnel," he added. "Different things are used to mix up the bad guy."The exact nature of the perceived threat to the aircraft in this latest case remains unclear. The Secret Service has so far not commented on the incident, while the White House has neither confirmed nor denied it, saying only that it uses every tool available to protect the president.While contingency plans for a variety of scenarios are developed ahead of time, experts say that the Secret Service needs to maintain flexibility and remain poised to improvise in the face of new threats as they emerge, particularly overseas.But according to McDonald, the extraordinary measure of secretly moving President Trump from the aircraft suggests that the potential danger was deemed, likely by multiple agencies, to be serious."That tells me that the threat level in Turkey was relatively substantial and quite high," he said, adding that the president's staff, the Secret Service and the White House Military Office were almost certainly immediately alerted."Those people likely got together in a room and were presented with this intelligence," McDonald explained. "And a plan was put together to negate the threat from whatever intelligence was received."McDonald's assessment was echoed by Marc Polymeropoulos, a 26-year veteran of the CIA who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan and oversaw clandestine missions around the world."The key part of this is the nature of the threat, and what was so severe that the Secret Service would put forth such a deception operation," he said.A key question going forward, according to Polymeropoulos, is whether the government and intelligence community then had a duty to warn those on the aircraft."Let's say the plane was blown out of the sky, and we knew about it," he said. "We don't do that…we can't. If we know ISIS is going to attack a target in Moscow, we warn the Russians. Why do we warn the Russians? Because if there's an American citizen killed in that, we can't let that happen."How much danger those who remained on the aircraft were in - or whether they were in danger at all - remains unclear.Journalists on board reported that they were repeatedly instructed to keep their window blinds down, a "not uncommon" practice McDonald said shows that steps were still being taken to protect the passengers."A large plane flying overhead where somebody could see it, with the shades up and windows illuminated, could tell somebody that it's a particular type of aircraft," he said. "I appreciate the need for transparency, but [the passengers] are also part of the roadshow. We've got to make sure that you and everybody gets home safe."The Secret Service, he added, is under no legal obligation to inform of potential threats or detail operations being carried out to protect the president and his entourage. That decision would need to be made by the White House or other agencies."The Secret Service is not in the business of public relations," he said. "We're very good at keeping secrets, as our name says. Everybody doesn't need to know everything."

schema.headline: Inside the Secret Service 'shell game' to hide US presidents in plain sight

title: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors
description: Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building,
body: Efraín Gallego does not lose faith that his brother will be found alive, although when he speaks about him, trapped beneath the rubble of a building, his voice breaks and he swallows hard until he regains his composure."You feel anguish. Every time there is an alert about someone being alive, hope is reborn that we will find him," Gallego tells me emotionally.His 80-year-old brother was buried along with his wife when the Torres del Limonar building collapsed in Cali.This city in south-western Colombia is one of the hardest hit by the earthquake.The building has become a symbol of the tragedy in the country's third most populous city.Cali has more than two million inhabitants. According to Mayor Alejandro Éder, there are at least 95 dead.Under the scorching heat on Tuesday morning, Torres del Limonar is a shattered mountain of rubble, with mattresses, furniture, and belongings peeking out from the concrete.On top of the remains are rescuers and volunteers: "Silence! We are firefighters. If you can hear us, shout or make any noise."The phrase is repeated every time the teams dig deep enough to believe they may be close to a survivor.These are the moments when Gallego regains hope, but the seconds pass and no answers come from below.Velasco offers hope. "In the past I have participated in operations where we have pulled out survivors after seven days trapped.""Those who are meant to survive, survive. Nothing is written," he adds."I wanted to help from the very beginning."Amid his anguish, Gallego wants to acknowledge the work of ordinary citizens."We must mention all the people who have come to help with water, supplies, tools, equipment; there is a lot of collaboration. Volunteers are plentiful," he says.Alejandro Mahecha, 19, is one of those volunteers. He decided to come after spending the night safely with his family and overcoming the initial shock."I wanted to help from the very beginning. The earthquake affected my city and the homes of people I know. I came to this site because there has been a lot of talk about this building and the need for help here," the young man explains.

schema.headline: Anguish of Colombian brother at rubble of building being searched for earthquake survivors

title: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane 'Keffe D' Davis
description: The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-ye
body: The only suspect ever charged for the drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 is Duane "Keffe D" Davis. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang.He has pleaded not guilty.The BBC's journalist Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty explains what we know about the suspect.Read more about the case here.

title: Watch: Manila river surface covered in tide of rubbish
description: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated
body: Workers waded through a rubbish-filled river in Manila, collecting waste that washed in during days of heavy rain. The nine-day downpour, exacerbated by tropical storms, was equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas. It resulted in school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the capital. Floods, landslides and accidents driven by the rains killed at least 16 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday

schema.headline: Watch: Manila river surface covered in tide of rubbish
